demographics.trauma_type: Accidentally caused serious injury to another

Triggers.value: Undergoing a medical examination or procedure

Maladaptive Strategies.value: keep mind occupied all the time

Threat.value: I have difficulty falling asleep because I need to stay alert
Having strong negative feelings such as fear, horror, anger, guilt, or shame
Having strong physical reactions when something reminded you of the stressful experience

Memory.value: The memory feels like it is happening right now rather than something that is over
When the memory comes back it feels completely real across all my senses at once
I know what happened but I am unable to find words to describe it

Negative Appraisals.value: I can't trust that I will do the right thing
My life has been destroyed by the trauma
The event happened because of the way I acted

issues.item: Memory: Verbal Access: I can talk about what happened very easily.
issues.explanation: Within Memory, 'Feels Present Not Past' and 'Full Sensory Reliving' indicate highly intrusive, poorly contextualized trauma memory, which conflicts with 'Verbal Access: I can talk about what happened very easily.' These can sometimes coexist, but stated this strongly they pull in opposite directions and are hard to reconcile as the same memory profile.

issues.item: Threat: Watching Others: I watch other people closely for signs that they might harm me
issues.explanation: The Threat items depict pervasive fear of being physically attacked by other people ('watch other people closely', 'back to wall', 'stay alert at night'), which does not fit well with the trauma type of accidentally causing serious injury to another. For this trauma, threat is more plausibly guilt, condemnation, or fear of consequences, not generalized interpersonal danger.

issues.item: Threat: Back to Wall: I feel unsafe unless my back is against a wall where I can see the room
issues.explanation: 'Mirror Checking' is not well linked to the rest of the profile. Nothing in Triggers, Memory, Threat, or Negative Appraisals suggests appearance-focused concern, dissociation needing visual reassurance, or checking for injury; as selected, it appears clinically disconnected.

Mirror checking is hard to reconcile with the trauma type of accidentally causing serious injury to another; it more strongly suggests concerns about visible injury, appearance, or being followed, none of which are supported by the other nodes.

issues.item: Back to Wall: I feel unsafe unless my back is against a wall where I can see the room
issues.explanation: Back-to-wall hypervigilance and scanning the room imply an interpersonal or attack-related threat context. That is difficult to integrate with the rest of the profile, which centers on guilt, reliving, and self-blame after accidentally injuring someone rather than danger from other people.

vignette: Julian had been directing students toward the gymnasium doors when the heavy wooden partition gave way. He reached out to steady a teenager who was toppling toward the concrete floor, but his arm extended a fraction too wide, sending the girl’s shoulder into the sharp edge of a metal railing. The crack was audible. What had been a straightforward afternoon now carried a fractured collarbone, and Julian was certain the injury happened because of the way he acted. He replayed the exact moment over and over, convinced that a different angle, a softer push, would have spared her. As a school counselor, he navigated the campus hallways with a quiet unease, certain he could not trust that he would do the right thing when moments demanded action. The incident did not feel like a distant occurrence to him; it felt suspended in time, as if the girl’s fall were still unfolding. When the memory surfaced, it arrived completely, carrying the heavy thud of the wood, the sharp metallic tang of the railing, and the sudden gasp of the crowd. He knew what had occurred, yet he often found himself unable to find words to describe it, as though the experience lived behind his ribs rather than in his mind. Over the months that followed, Julian’s days became a series of careful maneuvers. In his counseling office, where he spent his hours mediating conflicts and reviewing student files, the smell of floor wax and antiseptic wipes quickly became a potent trigger. When a substitute teacher brought in a bottle of hand sanitizer that shared that same sharp, chemical scent, Julian felt his chest tighten and his pulse spike against his collarbone. He kept his mind occupied at all times, sorting through schedules, correcting grade adjustments, and speaking in steady tones to fill the quiet. He found himself avoiding police officers whenever they visited the campus for security drills, stepping into his office rather than engaging. At home, his wife noticed he slept lightly, resting with one arm draped over his eyes so he could stay alert to any shift in the room. He experienced strong negative emotions that bloomed without warning—waves of guilt for the girl’s missed track meet, anger at his own clumsiness, and a low, constant shame that his life had been destroyed by that single misstep. When reminders surfaced, his body reacted; his jaw clenched, his shoulders hunched, and his breath grew shallow. Stress gathered in the staff lounge and the parent conference rooms, and the memory simply sat alongside his daily routines. The accumulation of these days had worn down his usual composure. He continued to work as a school counselor, navigating student crises and administrative meetings, but the professional setting now felt like a constant test of his judgment. He avoided thinking about the event. Stress gathered in the staff lounge and the parent conference rooms, and the memory simply sat alongside his daily routines. When his own routine physical examination approached, the thought of lying on an adjustable table, the hum of the clinic, the pressure of a stethoscope, sent a familiar wave of physical reactivity through him. What finally brought him to seek help was not a single breakdown, but the quiet realization that he was no longer living; he was merely managing. He hoped to find a way to trust his own instincts again, to stop bracing for the next misstep, but what frightened him most was the possibility that he would never be able to separate himself from the memory, that the injury he caused would remain as present and demanding as the day it happened.
